An old, old sight, and yet somehow so young; aye, and not changed a wink since I first saw it, a boy, from the sand-hills of Nantucket! The same!—the same!—the same to Noah as to me. There’s a soft shower to leeward. Such lovely leewardings! They must lead somewhere—to something else than common land, more palmy than the palms. Leeward! the white whale goes that way; look to windward, then; the better if the bitterer quarter. But good bye, good bye, old mast-head! What’s this?—green? aye, tiny mosses in these warped cracks. No such green weather stains on Ahab’s head! There’s the difference now between man’s old age and matter’s. But aye, old mast, we both grow old together; sound in our hulls, though, are we not, my ship? Aye, minus a leg, that’s all. By heaven this dead wood has the better of my live flesh every way. I can’t compare with it; and I’ve known some ships made of dead trees outlast the lives of men made of the most vital stuff of vital fathers. What’s that he said? he should still go before me, my pilot; and yet to be seen again? But where? Will I have eyes at the bottom of the sea, supposing I descend those endless stairs? and all night I’ve been sailing from him, wherever he did sink to. Aye, aye, like many more thou told’st direful truth as touching thyself, O Parsee; but, Ahab, there thy shot fell short. Good-bye, mast-head—keep a good eye upon the whale, the while I’m gone. We’ll talk to-morrow, nay, to-night, when the white whale lies down there, tied by head and tail.”
He gave the word; and still gazing round him, was steadily lowered through the cloven blue air to the deck.

In due time the boats were lowered; but as standing in his shallop’s stern, Ahab just hovered upon the point of the descent, he waved to the mate,—who held one of the tackle-ropes on deck—and bade him pause.
“Starbuck!”
“Sir?”
“For the third time my soul’s ship starts upon this voyage, Starbuck.”
“Aye, sir, thou wilt have it so.”
“Some ships sail from their ports, and ever afterwards are missing, Starbuck!”
“Truth, sir: saddest truth.”
“Some men die at ebb tide; some at low water; some at the full of the flood;—and I feel now like a billow that’s all one crested comb, Starbuck. I am old;—shake hands with me, man.”
Their hands met; their eyes fastened; Starbuck’s tears the glue.
“Oh, my captain, my captain!—noble heart—go not—go not!—see, it’s a brave man that weeps; how great the agony of the persuasion then!”
“Lower away!”—cried Ahab, tossing the mate’s arm from him. “Stand by the crew!”
In an instant the boat was pulling round close under the stern.
“The sharks! the sharks!” cried a voice from the low cabin-window there; “O master, my master, come back!”
But Ahab heard nothing; for his own voice was high-lifted then; and the boat leaped on.

Yet the voice spake true; for scarce had he pushed from the ship, when numbers of sharks, seemingly rising from out the dark waters beneath the hull, maliciously snapped at the blades of the oars, every time they dipped in the water; and in this way accompanied the boat with their bites. It is a thing not uncommonly happening to the whale-boats in those swarming seas; the sharks at times apparently following them in the same prescient way that vultures hover over the banners of marching regiments in the east. But these were the first sharks that had been observed by the Pequod since the White Whale had been first descried; and whether it was that Ahab’s crew were all such tiger-yellow barbarians, and therefore their flesh more musky to the senses of the sharks—a matter sometimes well known to affect them,—however it was, they seemed to follow that one boat without molesting the others.

“Heart of wrought steel!” murmured Starbuck gazing over the side, and following with his eyes the receding boat—“canst thou yet ring boldly to that sight?—lowering thy keel among ravening sharks, and followed by them, open-mouthed to the chase; and this the critical third day?—For when three days flow together in one continuous intense pursuit; be sure the first is the morning, the second the noon, and the third the evening and the end of that thing—be that end what it may. Oh! my God! what is this that shoots through me, and leaves me so deadly calm, yet expectant,—fixed at the top of a shudder! Future things swim before me, as in empty outlines and skeletons; all the past is somehow grown dim. Mary, girl! thou fadest in pale glories behind me; boy! I seem to see but thy eyes grown wondrous blue. Strangest problems of life seem clearing; but clouds sweep between—Is my journey’s end coming? My legs feel faint; like his who has footed it all day. Feel thy heart,—beats it yet? Stir thyself, Starbuck!—stave it off—move, move! speak aloud!—Mast-head there! See ye my boy’s hand on the hill?—Crazed;—aloft there!—keep thy keenest eye upon the boats:—mark well the whale!—Ho! again!—drive off that hawk! see! he pecks—he tears the vane”—pointing to the red flag flying at the main-truck—“Ha! he soars away with it!—Where’s the old man now? see’st thou that sight, oh Ahab!—shudder, shudder!”

The boats had not gone very far, when by a signal from the mast-heads—a downward pointed arm, Ahab knew that the whale had sounded; but intending to be near him at the next rising, he held on his way a little sideways from the vessel; the becharmed crew maintaining the profoundest silence, as the head-beat waves hammered and hammered against the opposing bow.
“Drive, drive in your nails, oh ye waves! to their uttermost heads drive them in! ye but strike a thing without a lid; and no coffin and no hearse can be mine:—and hemp only can kill me! Ha! ha!”

Suddenly the waters around them slowly swelled in broad circles; then quickly upheaved, as if sideways sliding from a submerged berg of ice, swiftly rising to the surface. A low rumbling sound was heard; a subterraneous hum; and then all held their breaths; as bedraggled with trailing ropes, and harpoons, and lances, a vast form shot lengthwise, but obliquely from the sea. Shrouded in a thin drooping veil of mist, it hovered for a moment in the rainbowed air; and then fell swamping back into the deep. Crushed thirty feet upwards, the waters flashed for an instant like heaps of fountains, then brokenly sank in a shower of flakes, leaving the circling surface creamed like new milk round the marble trunk of the whale.

“Give way!” cried Ahab to the oarsmen, and the boats darted forward to the attack; but maddened by yesterday’s fresh irons that corroded in him, Moby Dick seemed combinedly possessed by all the angels that fell from heaven. The wide tiers of welded tendons overspreading his broad white forehead, beneath the transparent skin, looked knitted together; as head on, he came churning his tail among the boats; and once more flailed them apart; spilling out the irons and lances from the two mates’ boats, and dashing in one side of the upper part of their bows, but leaving Ahab’s almost without a scar.

While Daggoo and Queequeg were stopping the strained planks; and as the whale swimming out from them, turned, and showed one entire flank as he shot by them again; at that moment a quick cry went up. Lashed round and round to the fish’s back; pinioned in the turns upon turns in which, during the past night, the whale had reeled the involutions of the lines around him, the half torn body of the Parsee was seen; his sable raiment frayed to shreds; his distended eyes turned full upon old Ahab.
The harpoon dropped from his hand.

“Befooled, befooled!”—drawing in a long lean breath—“Aye, Parsee! I see thee again.—Aye, and thou goest before; and this, _this_ then is the hearse that thou didst promise. But I hold thee to the last letter of thy word. Where is the second hearse? Away, mates, to the ship! those boats are useless now; repair them if ye can in time, and return to me; if not, Ahab is enough to die—Down, men! the first thing that but offers to jump from this boat I stand in, that thing I harpoon. Ye are not other men, but my arms and my legs; and so obey me.—Where’s the whale? gone down again?”

But he looked too nigh the boat; for as if bent upon escaping with the corpse he bore, and as if the particular place of the last encounter had been but a stage in his leeward voyage, Moby Dick was now again steadily swimming forward; and had almost passed the ship,—which thus far had been sailing in the contrary direction to him, though for the present her headway had been stopped. He seemed swimming with his utmost velocity, and now only intent upon pursuing his own straight path in the sea.
“Oh! Ahab,” cried Starbuck, “not too late is it, even now, the third day, to desist. See! Moby Dick seeks thee not. It is thou, thou, that madly seekest him!”

Setting sail to the rising wind, the lonely boat was swiftly impelled to leeward, by both oars and canvas. And at last when Ahab was sliding by the vessel, so near as plainly to distinguish Starbuck’s face as he leaned over the rail, he hailed him to turn the vessel about, and follow him, not too swiftly, at a judicious interval. Glancing upwards, he saw Tashtego, Queequeg, and Daggoo, eagerly mounting to the three mast-heads; while the oarsmen were rocking in the two staved boats which had but just been hoisted to the side, and were busily at work in repairing them. One after the other, through the port-holes, as he sped, he also caught flying glimpses of Stubb and Flask, busying themselves on deck among bundles of new irons and lances. As he saw all this; as he heard the hammers in the broken boats; far other hammers seemed driving a nail into his heart. But he rallied. And now marking that the vane or flag was gone from the main-mast-head, he shouted to Tashtego, who had just gained that perch, to descend again for another flag, and a hammer and nails, and so nail it to the mast.

Whether fagged by the three days’ running chase, and the resistance to his swimming in the knotted hamper he bore; or whether it was some latent deceitfulness and malice in him: whichever was true, the White Whale’s way now began to abate, as it seemed, from the boat so rapidly nearing him once more; though indeed the whale’s last start had not been so long a one as before. And still as Ahab glided over the waves the unpitying sharks accompanied him; and so pertinaciously stuck to the boat; and so continually bit at the plying oars, that the blades became jagged and crunched, and left small splinters in the sea, at almost every dip.
“Heed them not! those teeth but give new rowlocks to your oars. Pull on! ’tis the better rest, the shark’s jaw than the yielding water.”
“But at every bite, sir, the thin blades grow smaller and smaller!”

“They will last long enough! pull on!—But who can tell”—he muttered—“whether these sharks swim to feast on the whale or on Ahab?—But pull on! Aye, all alive, now—we near him. The helm! take the helm! let me pass,”—and so saying two of the oarsmen helped him forward to the bows of the still flying boat.

At length as the craft was cast to one side, and ran ranging along with the White Whale’s flank, he seemed strangely oblivious of its advance—as the whale sometimes will—and Ahab was fairly within the smoky mountain mist, which, thrown off from the whale’s spout, curled round his great, Monadnock hump; he was even thus close to him; when, with body arched back, and both arms lengthwise high-lifted to the poise, he darted his fierce iron, and his far fiercer curse into the hated whale. As both steel and curse sank to the socket, as if sucked into a morass, Moby Dick sideways writhed; spasmodically rolled his nigh flank against the bow, and, without staving a hole in it, so suddenly canted the boat over, that had it not been for the elevated part of the gunwale to which he then clung, Ahab would once more have been tossed into the sea. As it was, three of the oarsmen—who foreknew not the precise instant of the dart, and were therefore unprepared for its effects—these were flung out; but so fell, that, in an instant two of them clutched the gunwale again, and rising to its level on a combing wave, hurled themselves bodily inboard again; the third man helplessly dropping astern, but still afloat and swimming.

Almost simultaneously, with a mighty volition of ungraduated, instantaneous swiftness, the White Whale darted through the weltering sea. But when Ahab cried out to the steersman to take new turns with the line, and hold it so; and commanded the crew to turn round on their seats, and tow the boat up to the mark; the moment the treacherous line felt that double strain and tug, it snapped in the empty air!
“What breaks in me? Some sinew cracks!—’tis whole again; oars! oars! Burst in upon him!”

Hearing the tremendous rush of the sea-crashing boat, the whale wheeled round to present his blank forehead at bay; but in that evolution, catching sight of the nearing black hull of the ship; seemingly seeing in it the source of all his persecutions; bethinking it—it may be—a larger and nobler foe; of a sudden, he bore down upon its advancing prow, smiting his jaws amid fiery showers of foam.
Ahab staggered; his hand smote his forehead. “I grow blind; hands! stretch out before me that I may yet grope my way. Is’t night?”
“The whale! The ship!” cried the cringing oarsmen.

“Oars! oars! Slope downwards to thy depths, O sea, that ere it be for ever too late, Ahab may slide this last, last time upon his mark! I see: the ship! the ship! Dash on, my men! Will ye not save my ship?”

But as the oarsmen violently forced their boat through the sledge-hammering seas, the before whale-smitten bow-ends of two planks burst through, and in an instant almost, the temporarily disabled boat lay nearly level with the waves; its half-wading, splashing crew, trying hard to stop the gap and bale out the pouring water.

Meantime, for that one beholding instant, Tashtego’s mast-head hammer remained suspended in his hand; and the red flag, half-wrapping him as with a plaid, then streamed itself straight out from him, as his own forward-flowing heart; while Starbuck and Stubb, standing upon the bowsprit beneath, caught sight of the down-coming monster just as soon as he.

“The whale, the whale! Up helm, up helm! Oh, all ye sweet powers of air, now hug me close! Let not Starbuck die, if die he must, in a woman’s fainting fit. Up helm, I say—ye fools, the jaw! the jaw! Is this the end of all my bursting prayers? all my life-long fidelities? Oh, Ahab, Ahab, lo, thy work. Steady! helmsman, steady. Nay, nay! Up helm again! He turns to meet us! Oh, his unappeasable brow drives on towards one, whose duty tells him he cannot depart. My God, stand by me now!”

“Stand not by me, but stand under me, whoever you are that will now help Stubb; for Stubb, too, sticks here. I grin at thee, thou grinning whale! Who ever helped Stubb, or kept Stubb awake, but Stubb’s own unwinking eye? And now poor Stubb goes to bed upon a mattrass that is all too soft; would it were stuffed with brushwood! I grin at thee, thou grinning whale! Look ye, sun, moon, and stars! I call ye assassins of as good a fellow as ever spouted up his ghost. For all that, I would yet ring glasses with ye, would ye but hand the cup! Oh, oh! oh, oh! thou grinning whale, but there’ll be plenty of gulping soon! Why fly ye not, O Ahab! For me, off shoes and jacket to it; let Stubb die in his drawers! A most mouldy and over salted death, though;—cherries! cherries! cherries! Oh, Flask, for one red cherry ere we die!”
“Cherries? I only wish that we were where they grow. Oh, Stubb, I hope my poor mother’s drawn my part-pay ere this; if not, few coppers will now come to her, for the voyage is up.”

From the ship’s bows, nearly all the seamen now hung inactive; hammers, bits of plank, lances, and harpoons, mechanically retained in their hands, just as they had darted from their various employments; all their enchanted eyes intent upon the whale, which from side to side strangely vibrating his predestinating head, sent a broad band of overspreading semicircular foam before him as he rushed. Retribution, swift vengeance, eternal malice were in his whole aspect, and spite of all that mortal man could do, the solid white buttress of his forehead smote the ship’s starboard bow, till men and timbers reeled. Some fell flat upon their faces. Like dislodged trucks, the heads of the harpooneers aloft shook on their bull-like necks. Through the breach, they heard the waters pour, as mountain torrents down a flume.
“The ship! The hearse!—the second hearse!” cried Ahab from the boat; “its wood could only be American!”

Diving beneath the settling ship, the whale ran quivering along its keel; but turning under water, swiftly shot to the surface again, far off the other bow, but within a few yards of Ahab’s boat, where, for a time, he lay quiescent.

“I turn my body from the sun. What ho, Tashtego! let me hear thy hammer. Oh! ye three unsurrendered spires of mine; thou uncracked keel; and only god-bullied hull; thou firm deck, and haughty helm, and Pole-pointed prow,—death-glorious ship! must ye then perish, and without me? Am I cut off from the last fond pride of meanest shipwrecked captains? Oh, lonely death on lonely life! Oh, now I feel my topmost greatness lies in my topmost grief. Ho, ho! from all your furthest bounds, pour ye now in, ye bold billows of my whole foregone life, and top this one piled comber of my death! Towards thee I roll, thou all-destroying but unconquering whale; to the last I grapple with thee; from hell’s heart I stab at thee; for hate’s sake I spit my last breath at thee. Sink all coffins and all hearses to one common pool! and since neither can be mine, let me then tow to pieces, while still chasing thee, though tied to thee, thou damned whale! _Thus_, I give up the spear!”

The harpoon was darted; the stricken whale flew forward; with igniting velocity the line ran through the grooves;—ran foul. Ahab stooped to clear it; he did clear it; but the flying turn caught him round the neck, and voicelessly as Turkish mutes bowstring their victim, he was shot out of the boat, ere the crew knew he was gone. Next instant, the heavy eye-splice in the rope’s final end flew out of the stark-empty tub, knocked down an oarsman, and smiting the sea, disappeared in its depths.

For an instant, the tranced boat’s crew stood still; then turned. “The ship? Great God, where is the ship?” Soon they through dim, bewildering mediums saw her sidelong fading phantom, as in the gaseous Fata Morgana; only the uppermost masts out of water; while fixed by infatuation, or fidelity, or fate, to their once lofty perches, the pagan harpooneers still maintained their sinking lookouts on the sea. And now, concentric circles seized the lone boat itself, and all its crew, and each floating oar, and every lance-pole, and spinning, animate and inanimate, all round and round in one vortex, carried the smallest chip of the Pequod out of sight.

But as the last whelmings intermixingly poured themselves over the sunken head of the Indian at the mainmast, leaving a few inches of the erect spar yet visible, together with long streaming yards of the flag, which calmly undulated, with ironical coincidings, over the destroying billows they almost touched;—at that instant, a red arm and a hammer hovered backwardly uplifted in the open air, in the act of nailing the flag faster and yet faster to the subsiding spar. A sky-hawk that tauntingly had followed the main-truck downwards from its natural home among the stars, pecking at the flag, and incommoding Tashtego there; this bird now chanced to intercept its broad fluttering wing between the hammer and the wood; and simultaneously feeling that etherial thrill, the submerged savage beneath, in his death-gasp, kept his hammer frozen there; and so the bird of heaven, with archangelic shrieks, and his imperial beak thrust upwards, and his whole captive form folded in the flag of Ahab, went down with his ship, which, like Satan, would not sink to hell till she had dragged a living part of heaven along with her, and helmeted herself with it.

Now small fowls flew screaming over the yet yawning gulf; a sullen white surf beat against its steep sides; then all collapsed, and the great shroud of the sea rolled on as it rolled five thousand years ago.

modern_en.title: Chapter 135 — The Chase.—Third Day
paragraphs: The third morning dawned fair and fresh, and once again the lone night-watchman at the fore-masthead was relieved by crowds of daytime lookouts, who dotted every mast and nearly every spar.
"Do you see him?" cried Ahab; but the whale was not yet in sight.

"In his infallible wake, though; just follow that wake, that's all. Helm there; steady, as you go and have been going. What a lovely day again! If it were a new-made world, made for a summer-house for the angels, and this morning the first of its throwing open to them, a fairer day could not dawn upon that world. Here's food for thought, if Ahab had time to think; but Ahab never thinks; he only feels, feels, feels; and that is tingling enough for mortal man! To think is audacity. God alone has that right and privilege. Thinking is, or ought to be, a coolness and a calmness; and our poor hearts throb, and our poor brains beat, too much for that. And yet I've sometimes thought my brain was very calm — frozen calm, this old skull cracks so, like a glass whose contents have turned to ice and shivered it. And still this hair is growing now; growing this moment, and heat must breed it; but no, it's like that sort of common grass that will grow anywhere, between the earthy clefts of Greenland ice or in Vesuvius lava. How the wild winds blow it; they whip it about me as the torn shreds of split sails lash the tossed ship they cling to. A vile wind that has no doubt blown before this through prison corridors and cells, and hospital wards, and aired them out, and now comes blowing here as innocent as fleeces. Away with it! — it's tainted. If I were the wind, I'd blow no more on such a wicked, miserable world. I'd crawl off somewhere to a cave, and slink there. And yet the wind is a noble and heroic thing! Who ever conquered it? In every fight it has the last and bitterest blow. Run tilting at it, and you only run through it. Ha! a coward wind that strikes stark-naked men, but will not stand to receive a single blow. Even Ahab is a braver thing — a nobler thing than that. If only the wind had a body now; but all the things that most exasperate and outrage mortal man, all these things are bodiless — but bodiless only as objects, not as agents. There's a most special, a most cunning, oh, a most malicious difference! And yet, I say again, and swear it now, that there's something all glorious and gracious in the wind. These warm Trade Winds, at least, that blow straight on in the clear heavens, in strong and steadfast, vigorous mildness, and do not veer from their mark, however the baser currents of the sea may turn and tack, and the mightiest Mississippis of the land rush and swerve about, uncertain where to go at last. And by the eternal Poles! these same Trades that blow my good ship on so directly — these Trades, or something like them — something as unchangeable, and just as strong, blow my keeled soul along! To it! Aloft there! What do you see?"
"Nothing, sir."

"Nothing! And noon at hand! The doubloon goes begging! Look at the sun! Aye, aye, it must be so. I've oversailed him. How? Did he get the start? Aye, he's chasing me now — not I chasing him; that's bad; I might have known it, too. Fool! The lines — the harpoons he's towing. Aye, aye, I ran past him last night. About! About! Come down, all of you, except the regular lookouts! Man the braces!"

Because of the way she had been steering, the wind had been somewhat on the Pequod's quarter; so now, pointed in the reverse direction, the braced ship sailed close to the wind as she churned up again the cream of her own white wake.

"Against the wind he now steers for the open jaw," murmured Starbuck to himself, as he coiled the newly hauled main-brace on the rail. "God keep us, but already my bones feel damp inside me, and they wet my flesh from within. I fear that I disobey my God in obeying him!"
"Stand by to sway me up!" cried Ahab, advancing to the hempen basket. "We should meet him soon."
"Aye, aye, sir," and at once Starbuck did Ahab's bidding, and once more Ahab swung on high.

A whole hour now passed, beaten out like gold into ages. Time itself now held long breaths in keen suspense. But at last, some three points off the weather bow, Ahab sighted the spout again, and instantly three shrieks went up from the three mastheads, as if tongues of fire had voiced them.

"Forehead to forehead I meet you, this third time, Moby Dick! On deck there! — brace sharper up; crowd her into the wind's eye. He's too far off to lower yet, Mr. Starbuck. The sails shake! Stand over that helmsman with a top-maul! So, so; he travels fast, and I must go down. But let me have one more good round look aloft here at the sea; there's time for that. An old, old sight, and yet somehow so young; aye, and not changed a wink since I first saw it, a boy, from the sand-hills of Nantucket! The same! — the same! — the same to Noah as to me. There's a soft shower to leeward. Such lovely leewardings! They must lead somewhere — to something other than common land, more palmy than the palms. Leeward! The white whale goes that way; look to windward, then; the better if the bitterer quarter. But good-bye, good-bye, old masthead! What's this? — green? Aye, tiny mosses in these warped cracks. No such green weather-stains on Ahab's head! There's the difference now between man's old age and matter's. But aye, old mast, we both grow old together; sound in our hulls, though, are we not, my ship? Aye, minus a leg, that's all. By heaven, this dead wood has the better of my live flesh every way. I can't compare with it; and I've known some ships made of dead trees outlast the lives of men made of the most vital stuff of vital fathers. What's that he said? He should still go before me, my pilot, and yet be seen again? But where? Will I have eyes at the bottom of the sea, supposing I go down those endless stairs? And all night I've been sailing away from him, wherever he sank to. Aye, aye, like many more, you told dire truth about yourself, O Parsee; but, Ahab, there your shot fell short. Good-bye, masthead — keep a good eye on the whale while I'm gone. We'll talk tomorrow — no, tonight, when the white whale lies down there, tied by head and tail."
He gave the order, and, still looking all around him, was lowered steadily through the split blue air to the deck.

In due time the boats were lowered; but as Ahab, standing in the stern of his boat, hovered just at the point of descending, he waved to the mate — who held one of the tackle-ropes on deck — and told him to pause.
"Starbuck!"
"Sir?"
"For the third time my soul's ship sets out on this voyage, Starbuck."
"Aye, sir, you will have it so."
"Some ships sail from their ports and are missing ever afterward, Starbuck!"
"Truth, sir: saddest truth."
"Some men die at ebb tide; some at low water; some at the full of the flood; — and I feel now like a billow that's all one crested comb, Starbuck. I am old; — shake hands with me, man."
Their hands met; their eyes fastened; Starbuck's tears were the glue.
"Oh, my captain, my captain! — noble heart — don't go — don't go! — see, it's a brave man that weeps; how great, then, the agony of the pleading!"
"Lower away!" cried Ahab, tossing the mate's arm from him. "Stand by the crew!"
In an instant the boat was pulling round close under the stern.
"The sharks! The sharks!" cried a voice from the low cabin window there. "O master, my master, come back!"
But Ahab heard nothing, for just then his own voice was raised high; and the boat sprang on.

Yet the voice spoke true; for he had scarcely pushed off from the ship when numbers of sharks, seemingly rising out of the dark waters beneath the hull, snapped maliciously at the oar blades every time they dipped into the water, and in this way kept the boat company with their bites. It is a thing that not uncommonly happens to whaleboats in those swarming seas, the sharks at times apparently following them with the same foresight with which vultures hover over the banners of marching regiments in the east. But these were the first sharks the Pequod had observed since the White Whale was first sighted; and whether it was that Ahab's crew were all such tiger-yellow barbarians, and their flesh therefore more musky to the sharks' senses — a thing sometimes well known to affect them — however it was, they seemed to follow that one boat without molesting the others.

"Heart of wrought steel!" murmured Starbuck, gazing over the side and following the receding boat with his eyes — "can you still ring boldly to that sight? — lowering your keel among ravening sharks, and followed by them, open-mouthed, to the chase; and this the critical third day? — For when three days flow together in one continuous, intense pursuit, be sure the first is the morning, the second the noon, and the third the evening and the end of that thing — whatever that end may be. Oh, my God! what is this that shoots through me and leaves me so deadly calm, yet expectant — fixed at the top of a shudder! Future things swim before me, as in empty outlines and skeletons; all the past has somehow grown dim. Mary, girl! you fade in pale glories behind me; boy! I seem to see nothing of you but your eyes, grown wondrous blue. The strangest problems of life seem to be clearing; but clouds sweep between — Is my journey's end coming? My legs feel faint, like those of a man who has been on foot all day. Feel your heart — does it still beat? Stir yourself, Starbuck! — stave it off — move, move! Speak aloud! — Masthead there! Do you see my boy's hand on the hill? — Crazed; — aloft there! — keep your keenest eye on the boats — mark the whale well! — Ho! again! — drive off that hawk! See! he pecks — he tears the vane" — pointing to the red flag flying at the main-truck, the cap at the very top of the mainmast — "Ha! he soars away with it! — Where's the old man now? Do you see that sight, oh Ahab! — shudder, shudder!"

The boats had not gone very far when, by a signal from the mastheads — an arm pointed downward — Ahab knew that the whale had sounded; but meaning to be near him at his next rising, he held on his way a little to one side of the vessel, the spellbound crew keeping the deepest silence as the head-on waves hammered and hammered against the opposing bow.
"Drive, drive in your nails, oh you waves! Drive them in to their very heads! You only strike a thing without a lid; and no coffin and no hearse can be mine — and only hemp can kill me! Ha! ha!"

Suddenly the waters around them slowly swelled in broad circles; then quickly heaved up, as if sliding sideways off a submerged iceberg swiftly rising to the surface. A low rumbling sound was heard, a hum from under the earth; and then all held their breath, as, draggled with trailing ropes and harpoons and lances, a vast form shot lengthwise, but slantwise, from the sea. Shrouded in a thin, drooping veil of mist, it hovered for a moment in the rainbowed air, and then fell swamping back into the deep. Crushed thirty feet upward, the waters flashed for an instant like heaps of fountains, then sank brokenly in a shower of flakes, leaving the circling surface creamed like new milk round the marble trunk of the whale.

"Give way!" cried Ahab to the oarsmen, and the boats darted forward to the attack; but, maddened by yesterday's fresh irons corroding in him, Moby Dick seemed possessed by all the angels that fell from heaven at once. The wide tiers of welded tendons spreading over his broad white forehead beneath the transparent skin looked knitted together, as he came on head first, churning his tail among the boats, and once more flailed them apart, spilling the irons and lances out of the two mates' boats and smashing in one side of the upper part of their bows, but leaving Ahab's almost without a scar.

While Daggoo and Queequeg were stopping up the strained planks, and as the whale, swimming out from them, turned and showed one entire flank as he shot past them again, at that moment a quick cry went up. Lashed round and round to the fish's back, pinned in the turns upon turns in which the whale had wound the coils of the lines around himself during the past night, the half-torn body of the Parsee was seen, his black garments frayed to shreds, his bulging eyes turned full upon old Ahab.
The harpoon dropped from his hand.

"Fooled, fooled!" — drawing in a long, lean breath — "Aye, Parsee! I see you again. — Aye, and you go before; and this — this, then — is the hearse that you promised. But I hold you to the last letter of your word. Where is the second hearse? Away, mates, to the ship! Those boats are useless now; repair them if you can in time, and return to me; if not, Ahab is enough to die — Down, men! The first thing that so much as offers to jump from this boat I stand in, that thing I harpoon. You are not other men, but my arms and my legs; so obey me. — Where's the whale? Gone down again?"

But he looked too near the boat; for, as if bent on escaping with the corpse he carried, and as if the particular place of the last encounter had been only a stage in his voyage to leeward, Moby Dick was now again swimming steadily forward, and had almost passed the ship — which so far had been sailing in the opposite direction to him, though for the present her headway had been stopped. He seemed to be swimming at his utmost speed, and now intent only on pursuing his own straight path in the sea.
"Oh! Ahab," cried Starbuck, "it is not too late, even now, the third day, to stop. See! Moby Dick does not seek you. It is you, you, that madly seek him!"

Setting sail to the rising wind, the lonely boat was driven swiftly to leeward by both oars and canvas. And at last, as Ahab was sliding past the vessel, so near that he could plainly make out Starbuck's face as he leaned over the rail, he hailed him to turn the vessel about and follow him, not too swiftly, at a judicious interval. Glancing upward, he saw Tashtego, Queequeg, and Daggoo eagerly climbing to the three mastheads, while the oarsmen were rocking in the two staved boats, which had just been hoisted to the side, busily at work repairing them. One after another, through the portholes, as he sped by, he also caught flying glimpses of Stubb and Flask busying themselves on deck among bundles of new irons and lances. As he saw all this, as he heard the hammers in the broken boats, far different hammers seemed to be driving a nail into his heart. But he rallied. And now, noticing that the vane or flag was gone from the main-masthead, he shouted to Tashtego, who had just reached that perch, to come down again for another flag, and a hammer and nails, and so nail it to the mast.

Whether he was worn out by the three days' running chase and by the drag of the knotted tangle he carried, or whether it was some hidden deceitfulness and malice in him — whichever was true, the White Whale's speed now began, as it seemed from the boat so rapidly nearing him once more, to slacken; though indeed the whale's last start had not been so long a one as before. And still, as Ahab glided over the waves, the pitiless sharks went with him, and stuck so doggedly to the boat, and bit so continually at the plying oars, that the blades became jagged and crunched, and left small splinters in the sea at almost every dip.
"Pay them no heed! Those teeth only give your oars new rowlocks. Pull on! The shark's jaw is a better rest than the yielding water."
"But at every bite, sir, the thin blades grow smaller and smaller!"

"They will last long enough! Pull on! — But who can tell," he muttered, "whether these sharks swim to feast on the whale or on Ahab? — But pull on! Aye, all alive now — we're nearing him. The helm! Take the helm! Let me pass" — and with that, two of the oarsmen helped him forward to the bow of the still-flying boat.

At length, as the boat was cast to one side and ran along level with the White Whale's flank, he seemed strangely unaware of its approach — as the whale sometimes will be — and Ahab was right inside the smoky mountain of mist which, thrown off from the whale's spout, curled around his great Monadnock hump. He was that close to him when, with his body arched back and both arms raised high lengthwise to the poise, he darted his fierce iron, and his far fiercer curse, into the hated whale. As both steel and curse sank in to the socket, as if sucked into a morass, Moby Dick writhed sideways, rolled his near flank convulsively against the bow, and, without staving a hole in it, tipped the boat over so suddenly that, if it had not been for the raised part of the gunwale he then clung to, Ahab would once more have been thrown into the sea. As it was, three of the oarsmen — who had not known beforehand the exact instant of the dart, and were therefore unprepared for its effects — were flung out; but they fell in such a way that in an instant two of them clutched the gunwale again and, rising to its level on a combing wave, hurled themselves bodily back inboard; the third man dropped helplessly astern, but was still afloat and swimming.

Almost at the same moment, with a mighty act of will and a swiftness that came instantly, all at once, the White Whale darted through the weltering sea. But when Ahab called to the steersman to take new turns with the line and hold it so, and ordered the crew to turn round on their seats and tow the boat up to the mark, the moment the treacherous line felt that double strain and tug, it snapped in the empty air!
"What breaks in me? Some sinew cracks! — it's whole again; oars! oars! Burst in upon him!"

Hearing the tremendous rush of the sea-crashing boat, the whale wheeled round to present his blank forehead at bay; but in that turn, catching sight of the black hull of the ship drawing near, seemingly seeing in it the source of all his persecutions, taking it — it may be — for a larger and nobler foe, he suddenly bore down on its advancing prow, clashing his jaws amid fiery showers of foam.
Ahab staggered; his hand struck his forehead. "I'm growing blind; hands! stretch out before me so that I may still grope my way. Is it night?"
"The whale! The ship!" cried the cringing oarsmen.

"Oars! oars! Slope downward to your depths, O sea, so that before it is forever too late, Ahab may slide this last, last time upon his mark! I see: the ship! the ship! Dash on, my men! Will you not save my ship?"

But as the oarsmen violently forced their boat through the sledgehammering seas, the bow-ends of two planks that the whale had already struck burst through, and almost in an instant the temporarily disabled boat lay nearly level with the waves, its half-wading, splashing crew trying hard to stop the gap and bail out the pouring water.

Meanwhile, for that one instant of watching, Tashtego's masthead hammer stayed suspended in his hand; and the red flag, half wrapping him like a plaid, then streamed straight out from him, like his own forward-flowing heart; while Starbuck and Stubb, standing on the bowsprit below, caught sight of the oncoming monster just as soon as he did.

"The whale, the whale! Up helm, up helm! Oh, all you sweet powers of air, hold me close now! Let not Starbuck die, if die he must, in a woman's fainting fit. Up helm, I say — you fools, the jaw! the jaw! Is this the end of all my bursting prayers? all my lifelong fidelities? Oh, Ahab, Ahab, behold your work. Steady! helmsman, steady. No, no! Up helm again! He turns to meet us! Oh, his unappeasable brow drives on toward one whose duty tells him he cannot depart. My God, stand by me now!"

"Don't stand by me, but stand under me, whoever you are that will now help Stubb; for Stubb, too, sticks here. I grin at you, you grinning whale! Who ever helped Stubb, or kept Stubb awake, but Stubb's own unwinking eye? And now poor Stubb goes to bed on a mattress that is all too soft; I wish it were stuffed with brushwood! I grin at you, you grinning whale! Look here, sun, moon, and stars! I call you assassins of as good a fellow as ever spouted up his ghost. For all that, I would still clink glasses with you, if you would only hand the cup! Oh, oh! oh, oh! you grinning whale, but there'll be plenty of gulping soon! Why don't you fly, O Ahab! For me, off with shoes and jacket for it; let Stubb die in his drawers! A most moldy and oversalted death, though — cherries! cherries! cherries! Oh, Flask, for one red cherry before we die!"
"Cherries? I only wish that we were where they grow. Oh, Stubb, I hope my poor mother has drawn my part-pay before now; if not, few coppers will come to her now, for the voyage is up."

From the ship's bows nearly all the seamen now hung idle, hammers, bits of plank, lances, and harpoons still mechanically held in their hands, just as they had rushed from their various jobs; all their spellbound eyes were fixed on the whale, which, strangely swinging his predestinating head from side to side, sent a broad band of spreading, semicircular foam before him as he rushed. Retribution, swift vengeance, eternal malice were in his whole aspect, and in spite of all that mortal man could do, the solid white buttress of his forehead struck the ship's starboard bow, till men and timbers reeled. Some fell flat on their faces. Like dislodged trucks, the heads of the harpooners aloft shook on their bull-like necks. Through the breach they heard the waters pour, like mountain torrents down a flume.
"The ship! The hearse! — the second hearse!" cried Ahab from the boat. "Its wood could only be American!"

Diving beneath the settling ship, the whale ran quivering along its keel; but, turning under water, he shot swiftly to the surface again, far off the other bow, but within a few yards of Ahab's boat, where for a time he lay still.

"I turn my body from the sun. What ho, Tashtego! Let me hear your hammer. Oh! you three unsurrendered spires of mine; you uncracked keel; and only god-bullied hull; you firm deck, and haughty helm, and Pole-pointed prow — death-glorious ship! must you then perish, and without me? Am I cut off from the last fond pride of the meanest shipwrecked captains? Oh, lonely death on lonely life! Oh, now I feel my topmost greatness lies in my topmost grief. Ho, ho! from all your farthest bounds, pour in now, you bold billows of my whole bygone life, and top this one piled comber of my death! Toward you I roll, you all-destroying but unconquering whale; to the last I grapple with you; from hell's heart I stab at you; for hate's sake I spit my last breath at you. Sink all coffins and all hearses to one common pool! and since neither can be mine, let me then be towed to pieces, while still chasing you, though tied to you, you damned whale! Thus, I give up the spear!"

The harpoon was thrown; the wounded whale shot forward; the line ran through the grooves with igniting speed — and fouled. Ahab bent down to clear it; he did clear it; but the flying loop caught him around the neck, and as silently as Turkish mutes strangle their victim with the bowstring, he was jerked out of the boat before the crew knew he was gone. The next instant the heavy eye-splice at the very end of the rope flew out of the completely empty tub, knocked down an oarsman, and, hitting the sea, vanished into its depths.

For an instant the entranced boat's crew stood still; then turned. "The ship? Great God, where is the ship?" Soon, through dim, bewildering mediums, they saw her sidelong fading phantom, as in the gaseous Fata Morgana mirage, only the uppermost masts out of the water; while, fixed by infatuation, or fidelity, or fate to their once lofty perches, the pagan harpooners still kept their sinking lookouts on the sea. And now concentric circles seized the lone boat itself, and all its crew, and each floating oar, and every lance-pole, and, spinning animate and inanimate all round and round in one vortex, carried the smallest chip of the Pequod out of sight.

But as the last floods poured, mingling, over the sunken head of the Indian at the mainmast, leaving a few inches of the upright spar still visible, together with long streaming yards of the flag, which calmly rippled, with ironic coincidence, over the destroying billows they almost touched — at that instant a red arm and a hammer hovered, raised backward in the open air, in the act of nailing the flag faster and yet faster to the sinking spar. A sky-hawk that had tauntingly followed the main-truck downward from its natural home among the stars, pecking at the flag and harassing Tashtego there, now happened to put its broad fluttering wing between the hammer and the wood; and at the same moment, feeling that ethereal thrill, the submerged savage below, in his death-gasp, kept his hammer frozen there; and so the bird of heaven, with archangelic shrieks, his imperial beak thrust upward, and his whole captive form folded in the flag of Ahab, went down with his ship, which, like Satan, would not sink to hell until she had dragged a living part of heaven along with her and helmeted herself with it.

Now little birds flew screaming over the gulf, which still gaped open; a sullen white surf beat against its steep sides; then everything collapsed, and the great shroud of the sea rolled on as it had rolled five thousand years ago.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 135 — Jagten — Tredje dag
paragraphs: Den tredje morgen randt klar og frisk, og endnu en gang blev den ensomme natvagt i forreste mastetop afløst af mængder af dagudkig, der prikkede hver mast og næsten hver rå.
»Kan I se ham?« råbte Ahab. Men hvalen var endnu ikke i sigte.

»I hans ufejlbarlige kølvand dog. Følg bare det kølvand, det er det hele. Roret derovre, hold kursen, som du går og har gået. Hvor er det igen en dejlig dag! Hvis det var en nyskabt verden, skabt som lysthus for englene, og i morges første gang åbnet for dem, kunne en smukkere dag ikke gry over den verden. Her er stof til eftertanke, hvis Ahab havde tid til at tænke. Men Ahab tænker aldrig, han føler kun, føler, føler, og det er nok til at sitre af for et dødeligt menneske! At tænke er dristighed. Gud alene har den ret og det privilegium. Tænkning er, eller burde være, en kølighed og en ro. Og vore stakkels hjerter banker og vore stakkels hjerner hamrer for meget til det. Og alligevel har jeg undertiden troet, at min hjerne var meget rolig — frossen rolig. Denne gamle hjerneskal revner så, som et glas, hvis indhold er blevet til is og har sprængt det. Og alligevel gror dette hår nu, gror lige nu, og varme må føde det. Men nej, det er som den slags almindeligt græs, der vil gro hvor som helst, i jordsprækkerne i Grønlands is eller i Vesuvs lava. Hvor de vilde vinde blæser i det. De pisker det rundt om mig, som de sønderrevne stumper af flækkede sejl pisker det slingrende skib, de klamrer sig til. En væmmelig vind, som uden tvivl før nu har blæst gennem fængselsgange og celler og sygehusstuer og luftet dem ud, og nu kommer blæsende her så uskyldig som uldskind. Væk med den! — den er smittet. Hvis jeg var vinden, ville jeg ikke blæse mere over sådan en ond, elendig verden. Jeg ville krybe hen i en hule et sted og luske rundt dér. Og alligevel er vinden en ædel og heltemodig ting! Hvem har nogensinde besejret den? I hver kamp har den det sidste og bitreste slag. Gå løs på den med lanse, og du farer kun igennem den. Ha! en fej vind, der slår splitternøgne mænd, men ikke vil stå fast og modtage et eneste slag. Selv Ahab er en modigere ting — en ædlere ting end det. Hvis bare vinden havde en krop nu. Men alle de ting, der mest ophidser og krænker dødelige mennesker, alle disse ting er kropsløse — men kun kropsløse som genstande, ikke som handlende. Der er en højst særlig, en højst snedig, åh, en højst ondskabsfuld forskel! Og alligevel siger jeg igen, og sværger det nu, at der er noget helt herligt og nådigt i vinden. Disse varme passatvinde i det mindste, der blæser lige videre i den klare himmel, i stærk og standhaftig, kraftfuld mildhed, og ikke afviger fra deres mål, hvordan de lavere strømme i havet end vender og krydser, og landets mægtigste Mississippier styrter og slingrer rundt, usikre på, hvor de til sidst skal hen. Og ved de evige poler! disse samme passater, der blæser mit gode skib så lige frem — disse passater, eller noget der ligner dem — noget lige så uforanderligt og lige så stærkt — blæser min sjæl med køl under sig af sted! Til det! Hallo, deroppe! Hvad ser I?«
»Intet, sir.«

»Intet! Og middag lige om hjørnet! Doubloonen går tiggende! Se på solen! Ja, ja, det må være sådan. Jeg har sejlet forbi ham. Hvordan? Fik han et forspring? Ja, han jager mig nu — ikke jeg ham. Det er dårligt, det kunne jeg også have vidst. Tåbe! Linerne — harpunerne, han slæber på. Ja, ja, jeg løb forbi ham i nat. Klar til at vende! Klar til at vende! Kom ned, alle sammen, undtagen de faste udkig! Bemand brasserne!«

På grund af den kurs, hun havde styret, havde vinden ligget lidt ind på Pequods agterkvarter. Så nu, vendt i den modsatte retning, sejlede det brassede skib tæt op mod vinden, mens hun igen pløjede fløden i sit eget hvide kølvand op.

»Mod vinden styrer han nu mod det åbne gab,« mumlede Starbuck for sig selv, mens han klarerede det nyligt halede stor-brasserep på rælingen. »Gud beskytte os, men allerede føles mine knogler fugtige inde i mig, og de gør mit kød vådt indefra. Jeg frygter, at jeg ulyder min Gud ved at adlyde ham!«
»Gør klar til at svinge mig op!« råbte Ahab og gik hen til den hampeflettede kurv. »Vi skulle snart møde ham.«
»Ja, ja, sir,« og straks gjorde Starbuck, som Ahab bød, og endnu en gang svingede Ahab højt til vejrs.

Nu gik der en hel time, slået ud som guld til aldre. Selve tiden holdt vejret i lange, spændte åndedrag. Men til sidst, omkring tre streger ude for den luvvendte bov, fik Ahab øje på blæsten igen, og med det samme lød der tre skrig fra de tre mastetoppe, som om ildtunger havde udstødt dem.

»Pande mod pande møder jeg dig, denne tredje gang, Moby Dick! Hør dér på dækket — brasse skarpere op, pres hende ind i vindens øje. Han er for langt væk til, at vi kan sætte bådene ud endnu, Mr. Starbuck. Sejlene slår! Stil dig over rorgængeren med en tophammer! Så, så, han svømmer hurtigt, og jeg må ned. Men lad mig få et ordentligt blik rundt over havet her oppefra; der er tid til det. Et gammelt, gammelt syn, og alligevel på en eller anden måde så ungt. Ja, og uændret en tøddel, siden jeg første gang så det som dreng fra sandbakkerne på Nantucket! Det samme! — det samme! — det samme for Noah som for mig. Der er en blød byge i læ. Sikke dejlige lesider! De må føre et sted hen — til noget andet end almindeligt land, mere palmegrønt end palmerne. Læ! Dér går den hvide hval; så se mod luv, så meget bedre, hvis det er den bitreste kant. Men farvel, farvel, gamle mastetop! Hvad er dét? — grønt? Ja, små mosser i de skæve sprækker her. Der er ingen sådanne grønne vejrpletter på Ahabs hoved! Dér har vi forskellen mellem menneskets alderdom og tingenes. Men ja, gamle mast, vi bliver gamle sammen; sunde i skroget er vi dog, ikke sandt, mit skib? Ja, bortset fra et ben, det er det hele. Ved himlen, dette døde træ har det bedre end mit levende kød på alle måder. Jeg kan ikke måle mig med det; og jeg har kendt skibe bygget af døde træer, der overlevede mænd, som var lavet af det mest levende stof fra levende fædre. Hvad var det, han sagde? At han stadig skulle gå foran mig, min lods, og dog blive set igen? Men hvor? Vil jeg have øjne på havets bund, hvis jeg går ned ad de endeløse trapper? Og hele natten har jeg sejlet bort fra ham, uanset hvor han sank hen. Ja, ja, som mange andre sagde du frygtelige sandheder om dig selv, o parsi; men Ahab, dér faldt dit skud for kort. Farvel, mastetop — hold et godt øje med hvalen, mens jeg er væk. Vi skal tale sammen i morgen — nej, i nat, når den hvide hval ligger dernede, bundet i hoved og hale.«
Han gav ordren, og mens han stadig så sig rundt, blev han firet jævnt ned gennem den kløvede, blå luft til dækket.

I rette tid blev bådene sat ud. Men netop som Ahab, stående i agterstavnen på sin båd, svævede netop på nippet til at gå ned, vinkede han til styrmanden — som på dækket holdt i et af taljerebene — og bad ham holde inde.
»Starbuck!«
»Ja, sir?«
»For tredje gang sætter min sjæls skib ud på denne rejse, Starbuck.«
»Ja, sir, De vil have det sådan.«
»Nogle skibe sejler fra deres havne og er forsvundet for evigt bagefter, Starbuck!«
»Sandt, sir: den sørgeligste sandhed.«
»Nogle mænd dør ved ebbe; nogle ved lavvande; nogle ved højeste flod; — og jeg føler mig nu som en bølge, der er én eneste kronet kam, Starbuck. Jeg er gammel; — giv mig hånden, mand.«
Deres hænder mødtes; deres øjne låste sig fast; Starbucks tårer var limen.
»Åh, min kaptajn, min kaptajn! — ædle hjerte — lad være at tage af sted — lad være! — se, det er en modig mand, der græder; hvor stor må så ikke kvalen være ved at trygle!«
»Fire ned!« råbte Ahab og slyngede styrmandens arm fra sig. »Mandskabet på plads!«
I et øjeblik roede båden rundt tæt under agterenden.
»Hajerne! Hajerne!« råbte en stemme fra det lave kahytsvindue dér. »O herre, min herre, kom tilbage!«
Men Ahab hørte intet, for netop da var hans egen stemme hævet højt, og båden fór af sted.

Alligevel havde stemmen talt sandt. For han havde næsten ikke skubbet fra skibet, før en mængde hajer, der tilsyneladende steg op af det mørke vand under skroget, ondskabsfuldt bed efter årebladene, hver gang de dykkede ned i vandet, og på den måde fulgte båden med deres bid. Det er noget, der ikke sjældent sker for hvalbåde i de vrimlende have, hvor hajerne til tider tilsyneladende følger dem med samme forudseende, som gribbe svæver over de marcherende regimenters faner i østen. Men det var de første hajer, Pequod havde set, siden den hvide hval blev opdaget første gang. Og hvad enten det nu var, fordi Ahabs mandskab alle sammen var sådanne tigergule barbarer, så deres kød smagte mere af moskus for hajernes sanser — noget, der somme tider vides at påvirke dem — så var det i hvert fald sådan, at de syntes at følge den ene båd uden at genere de andre.

»Hjerte af smedet stål!« mumlede Starbuck, mens han så ud over rælingen og fulgte den bortglidende båd med øjnene — »kan du stadig ringe frimodigt ved det syn? — sænke dit køl ned blandt glubske hajer og blive fulgt af dem med åbne kæber ud på jagten; og det på den afgørende tredje dag? — For når tre dage flyder sammen til én uafbrudt, intens forfølgelse, så vær sikker på, at den første er morgenen, den anden middagen og den tredje aftenen og enden på den sag — hvad enden så end bliver. Åh, min Gud! Hvad er det, der skyder gennem mig og gør mig så dødeligt rolig, men afventende — stivnet på toppen af et gys! Kommende ting svømmer foran mig som tomme omrids og skeletter; alt det forgangne er på en eller anden måde blevet dunkelt. Mary, min pige! Du blegner i svage glorier bag mig; dreng! Jeg synes ikke at se andet af dig end dine øjne, der er blevet forunderligt blå. Livets mærkeligste gåder synes at klare op; men skyer fejer imellem — Er min rejses ende ved at komme? Mine ben føles svage, som hos en mand, der har gået hele dagen. Føl dit hjerte — slår det stadig? Rør dig, Starbuck! — hold det fra livet — bevæg dig, bevæg dig! Tal højt! — Mastetop dér! Kan du se min drengs hånd på bakken? — Vanvittigt; — op dér! — hold dit skarpeste øje på bådene — mærk hvalen godt! — Hej! igen! — jag den høg væk! Se! Han hakker — han river vimplen af« — idet han pegede på det røde flag, der vajede ved stormastens top, kappen helt øverst på stormasten — »Ha! Han svinger sig væk med den! — Hvor er den gamle nu? Ser du det syn, o Ahab! — gys, gys!«

Bådene var ikke nået ret langt, da Ahab ved et signal fra mastetoppene — en arm, der pegede nedad — vidste, at hvalen var dykket. Men da han ville være i nærheden, når den steg op næste gang, holdt han sin kurs et stykke til siden af skibet, mens det fortryllede mandskab holdt den dybeste tavshed, og de modgående bølger hamrede og hamrede mod den modstående bov.
»Slå, slå sømmene i, o I bølger! Slå dem i helt til hovederne! I rammer kun noget uden låg; og ingen ligkiste og ingen ligvogn kan blive min — og kun hamp kan dræbe mig! Ha! ha!«

Pludselig svulmede vandet omkring dem langsomt i brede kredse; så hævede det sig hurtigt, som om det gled sidelæns af et nedsænket isbjerg, der hurtigt steg op mod overfladen. En dump rumlen blev hørt, en summen fra under jorden. Og så holdt alle vejret, for tilsmudset af slæbende liner og harpuner og lanser skød en vældig skikkelse på langs, men på skrå, op af havet. Indhyllet i et tyndt, hængende dække af tåge svævede den et øjeblik i den regnbuefarvede luft og faldt så, oversvømmende alt omkring sig, tilbage i dybet. Knust tredive fod opad glimtede vandet et øjeblik som hobe af springvand og sank så sønderbrudt ned i et skur af flager. Tilbage lå den kredsende overflade flødet som ny mælk rundt om hvalens marmorstamme.

»Træk til!« råbte Ahab til roerne, og bådene skød frem til angrebet. Men gjort vanvittig af gårsdagens friske jern, der åd sig ind i ham, virkede Moby Dick besat af alle englene, der faldt fra himlen på én gang. De brede lag af sammensvejsede sener, der bredte sig over hans brede hvide pande under den gennemsigtige hud, lignede noget, der var strikket sammen, da han kom frem med hovedet først, pidskede med halen blandt bådene og endnu en gang slog dem fra hinanden, så jernene og lanserne væltede ud af de to styrmænds både og den øverste del af deres stævne blev smadret på den ene side. Men Ahabs båd efterlod han næsten uden et mærke.

Mens Daggoo og Queequeg stoppede de anstrengte planker til, og mens hvalen, der svømmede væk fra dem, vendte sig og viste hele den ene side, da den igen skød forbi dem, lød i det øjeblik et hurtigt råb. Surret rundt og rundt på fiskens ryg, fastklemt i de ture på ture, hvormed hvalen i løbet af den forgangne nat havde viklet linernes snoninger omkring sig, kunne man se parsiens halvt sønderrevne legeme, hans sorte klæder flosset i laser, hans udstående øjne vendt lige mod gamle Ahab.
Harpunen faldt ud af hans hånd.

»Narret, narret!« — idet han trak et langt, magert åndedrag — »Ja, parsi! Jeg ser dig igen. — Ja, og du går foran; og dette — dette er altså den ligvogn, du lovede. Men jeg holder dig til dit ords sidste bogstav. Hvor er den anden ligvogn? Væk, mænd, til skibet! De både er til ingen nytte nu; reparer dem, hvis I kan nå det i tide, og kom tilbage til mig; hvis ikke, er Ahab nok til at dø — Ned, mænd! Det første, der så meget som gør mine til at hoppe fra denne båd, som jeg står i, det harpunerer jeg. I er ikke andre mænd, men mine arme og mine ben; så adlyd mig. — Hvor er hvalen? Gået ned igen?«

Men han kiggede for nær ved båden. For som om han var opsat på at slippe væk med det lig, han bar, og som om stedet for det sidste sammenstød kun havde været en etape på hans rejse mod læ, svømmede Moby Dick nu igen støt fremad og var næsten svømmet forbi skibet — som hidtil havde sejlet i modsat retning af ham, skønt hendes fart for øjeblikket var blevet standset. Han syntes at svømme for fuld kraft og nu kun at være opsat på at følge sin egen lige vej i havet.
»Åh! Ahab,« råbte Starbuck, »det er ikke for sent, selv nu, på tredje dag, at holde inde. Se! Moby Dick søger ikke Dem. Det er Dem, Dem, der vanvittigt søger ham!«

Idet den ensomme båd satte sejl for den stigende vind, blev den drevet hurtigt mod læ af både årer og sejldug. Og til sidst, da Ahab gled forbi skibet, så nær at han tydeligt kunne se Starbucks ansigt, mens denne lænede sig over rælingen, råbte han til ham, at han skulle vende skibet og følge efter ham, ikke for hurtigt, med et fornuftigt mellemrum. Da han så op, så han Tashtego, Queequeg og Daggoo ivrigt klatre op til de tre mastetoppe, mens roerne gyngede i de to flækkede både, som lige var blevet hejst op til siden, og travlt arbejdede med at reparere dem. Gennem lugerne fik han også, mens han fór forbi, flygtige glimt af Stubb og Flask, som travlt gik rundt på dækket blandt bundter af nye jern og lanser. Da han så alt dette og hørte hamrene i de ødelagte både, syntes helt andre hamre at drive et søm ind i hans hjerte. Men han tog sig sammen. Og da han nu lagde mærke til, at vimplen eller flaget var væk fra stormastens top, råbte han til Tashtego, som netop var nået op på det sted, at han skulle komme ned igen efter et nyt flag og en hammer og søm og så sømme det fast til masten.

Hvad enten han var udmattet af tre dages løbende jagt og af slæbet fra den knudrede floke, han bar på, eller det var en skjult svigefuldhed og ondskab hos ham — hvad der end var sandt, begyndte den hvide hvals fart nu, som det virkede fra båden, der igen nærmede sig ham så hurtigt, at aftage. Dog havde hvalens sidste stød ikke været så langt som før. Og stadig fulgte de ubarmhjertige hajer med Ahab, mens han gled over bølgerne, og de holdt sig så hårdnakket til båden og bed så uafbrudt i de arbejdende årer, at bladene blev takkede og knasede og efterlod små splinter i havet næsten ved hvert dyk.
»Tag jer ikke af dem! De tænder giver bare jeres årer nye åregafler. Træk til! Hajens kæbe er en bedre støtte end det eftergivende vand.«
»Men ved hvert bid, sir, bliver de tynde blade mindre og mindre!«

»De holder længe nok! Træk til! — Men hvem ved,« mumlede han, »om disse hajer svømmer for at æde hvalen eller Ahab? — Men træk til! Ja, alle levende nu — vi nærmer os ham. Roret! Tag roret! Lad mig komme forbi« — og med det hjalp to af roerne ham frem til stævnen af den stadig flyvende båd.

Til sidst, da båden blev kastet til den ene side og løb side om side med den hvide hvals flanke, syntes han mærkeligt uvidende om dens nærmelse — som hvalen undertiden er — og Ahab var lige inde i det rygende bjerg af tåge, der, kastet af hvalens blæst, krøllede sig om hans store Monadnock-pukkel. Så tæt var han på ham, da han med kroppen buet tilbage og begge arme løftet højt på langs til kastet sendte sit vilde jern og sin langt vildere forbandelse ind i den hadede hval. Mens både stål og forbandelse sank ind til skaftet, som om de blev suget ned i en mose, vred Moby Dick sig til siden, rullede sin nærmeste flanke krampagtigt mod stævnen og væltede båden så pludseligt, uden at slå hul i den, at Ahab, hvis det ikke havde været for den forhøjede del af rælingen, som han da klamrede sig til, endnu en gang var blevet kastet i havet. Som det gik, blev tre af roerne — som ikke på forhånd havde kendt det nøjagtige øjeblik for kastet og derfor var uforberedte på dets virkninger — slynget ud. Men de faldt sådan, at to af dem i et øjeblik greb fat i rælingen igen og, stigende op til dens højde på en brydende bølge, kastede sig helt ind i båden igen. Den tredje faldt hjælpeløst agterud, men var stadig oven vande og svømmede.

Næsten i samme øjeblik skød den hvide hval af sted gennem det oprørte hav med en vældig viljesanstrengelse og en fart, der kom på et splitsekund. Men da Ahab råbte til rorgængeren, at han skulle tage nye tørn med linen og holde den sådan, og befalede mandskabet at vende sig om på tofterne og hale båden op til mærket, så snart den forræderiske line mærkede det dobbelte træk og ryk, knækkede den i den tomme luft!
»Hvad brister i mig? En sene knækker! — nu er den hel igen. Årerne! Årerne! Kast jer over ham!«

Da hvalen hørte den vældige susen fra den havbrydende båd, drejede den rundt for at vise sin tomme pande, så den stod for skud. Men i den drejning fik den øje på skibets sorte skrog, der kom nærmere. Tilsyneladende så den i det kilden til alle sine forfølgelser og tog det måske for en større og ædlere fjende. Pludselig stævnede den mod den fremadskridende forstavn og klaprede med kæberne midt i flammende byger af skum.
Ahab vaklede, og hans hånd slog mod panden. »Jeg er ved at blive blind. Hænder! Stræk jer ud foran mig, så jeg stadig kan famle mig frem. Er det nat?«
»Hvalen! Skibet!« råbte de sammenkrøbne roere.

»Årerne! Årerne! Skrån nedad til dine dybder, o hav, så Ahab, før det for evigt er for sent, kan glide denne sidste, sidste gang hen til sit mærke! Jeg ser det: skibet! skibet! Frem med jer, mine mænd! Vil I da ikke redde mit skib?«

Men mens roerne drev deres båd voldsomt gennem de hammerslående bølger, sprang enderne af to planker ved forstavnen, som hvalen allerede havde ramt, op. Og næsten på et øjeblik lå den midlertidigt ødelagte båd næsten i niveau med bølgerne, mens den halvt vadende, pjaskende besætning kæmpede for at stoppe hullet og øse det strømmende vand ud.

Imens hang Tashtegos hammer i dette ene øjebliks udkig stille i hans hånd, og det røde flag, der halvt havde svøbt sig om ham som en plaid, strakte sig nu lige ud fra ham som hans eget fremadstrømmende hjerte. Starbuck og Stubb, der stod på bovsprydet nedenfor, fik øje på det frembrusende uhyre lige så hurtigt som han.

»Hvalen, hvalen! Roret i læ, roret i læ! Åh, alle I milde kræfter i luften, hold mig fast nu! Lad ikke Starbuck dø, hvis han skal dø, i et kvindeligt vanmagtsanfald. Roret i læ, siger jeg — I tåber, kæben! kæben! Er det enden på alle mine brændende bønner? På al min trofasthed gennem et helt liv? Åh, Ahab, Ahab, se, hvad du har gjort. Hold kursen! Rorgænger, hold kursen. Nej, nej! Roret i læ igen! Han drejer for at møde os! Åh, hans uforsonlige pande styrer ind mod en, hvis pligt siger ham, at han ikke kan gå sin vej. Min Gud, stå mig bi nu!«

»Stå mig ikke bi, men stå under mig, hvem du end er, der nu vil hjælpe Stubb. For Stubb sidder også fast her. Jeg griner af dig, din grinende hval! Hvem har nogensinde hjulpet Stubb eller holdt Stubb vågen andet end Stubbs eget søvnløse øje? Og nu går stakkels Stubb i seng på en madras, der er alt for blød. Gid den var stoppet med ris! Jeg griner af dig, din grinende hval! Se her, sol, måne og stjerner! Jeg kalder jer snigmordere på en så god fyr, som nogensinde har pustet sin ånd ud. Alligevel ville jeg stadig skåle med jer, hvis I bare ville række bægeret. Åh, åh! åh, åh! din grinende hval, men snart bliver der rigeligt at synke! Hvorfor flyver De ikke væk, Ahab! Hvad mig angår: af med sko og jakke, lad Stubb dø i underbukserne! En højst muggen og oversaltet død — kirsebær! kirsebær! kirsebær! Åh, Flask, ét rødt kirsebær, før vi dør!«
»Kirsebær? Gid vi bare var der, hvor de gror. Åh, Stubb, jeg håber, min stakkels mor har hævet min delvise løn nu. Hvis ikke, kommer der kun få mønter til hende, for rejsen er ude.«

Fra skibets stævn hang næsten alle sømændene nu ubevægelige, med hamre, stykker af planker, lanser og harpuner stadig mekanisk i hænderne, ligesom de var styrtet af sted fra deres forskellige arbejder. Alle deres fortryllede øjne var rettet mod hvalen, der underligt svingede sit skæbnebestemmende hoved fra side til side og sendte et bredt bælte af udbredende, halvrundt skum foran sig, mens den fór frem. Gengældelse, hurtig hævn og evig ondskab lå i hele dens skikkelse, og trods alt, hvad et dødeligt menneske kunne gøre, ramte den solide hvide støttepille af en pande skibets styrbords bov, så mænd og planker rystede. Nogle faldt på ansigtet. Som løsnede mastknopper rystede harpunerernes hoveder deroppe på deres tyrenakker. Gennem hullet hørte de vandet strømme ind som bjergfloder ned ad en rende.
»Skibet! Ligvognen! — den anden ligvogn!« råbte Ahab fra båden. »Dens træ kunne kun være amerikansk!«

Hvalen dykkede under det synkende skib og løb skælvende langs dets køl. Men den vendte under vandet og skød hurtigt op til overfladen igen, langt borte ved den anden bov, men kun nogle få yard fra Ahabs båd, hvor den lå stille et stykke tid.

»Jeg vender min krop bort fra solen. Hallo, Tashtego! Lad mig høre din hammer. Åh! Mine tre uovervundne spir; du ubrudte køl og kun af guder plagede skrog; du faste dæk og stolte ror og polvendte forstavn — dødsberømte skib! Skal du så gå under, og det uden mig? Er jeg afskåret fra den sidste kære stolthed hos selv de ringeste forliste kaptajner? Åh, ensom død på ensomt liv! Åh, nu mærker jeg, at min højeste storhed ligger i min højeste sorg. Hej, hej! Væld nu ind fra jeres yderste grænser, I dristige bølger fra hele mit svundne liv, og top denne ene opstablede brådsø af min død! Mod dig ruller jeg, du altødelæggende, men uovervundne hval. Til det sidste kæmper jeg med dig. Fra helvedes hjerte stikker jeg til dig. For hadets skyld spytter jeg mit sidste åndedrag mod dig. Sænk alle kister og alle ligvogne i én fælles pøl! Og da ingen af dem kan blive min, så lad mig blive slæbt i stykker, mens jeg stadig jager dig, skønt bundet til dig, din forbandede hval! Således giver jeg spyddet op!«

Harpunen blev kastet. Den sårede hval skød frem, og linen løb gennem rillerne med en fart, der fik den til at ryge — og floker sig. Ahab bøjede sig ned for at klare den. Han klarede den, men den flyvende løkke fik fat om hans hals, og lige så lydløst, som tyrkiske stumme kvæler deres offer med buestrengen, blev han revet ud af båden, før besætningen vidste, at han var væk. I næste øjeblik fløj den tunge øjesplejsning for enden af tovet ud af den helt tomme balje, slog en roer ned og forsvandt i havets dyb, da den ramte det.

I et øjeblik stod den fortryllede bådbesætning stille. Så vendte de sig om. »Skibet? Store Gud, hvor er skibet?« Snart så de gennem dunkle, forvirrende luftlag dets skråt hensvindende genfærd, som i Fata Morgana-synet i gasagtig luft, med kun de øverste master oppe af vandet. Og fastholdt af vanvid eller troskab eller skæbne på deres engang så høje pladser holdt de hedenske harpunerere stadig deres synkende udkig over havet. Og nu greb koncentriske kredse den ensomme båd selv og hele dens besætning og hver eneste flydende åre og hver eneste lansestage. Og mens de snurrede alt levende og livløst rundt og rundt i én hvirvel, bar de den mindste splint af Pequod ud af syne.

Men da de sidste vandmasser strømmede sammen over indianerens nedsunkne hoved ved stormasten og kun nogle få tommer af den lodrette rundholt stod tilbage at se, sammen med lange vajende yard af flaget, som roligt bølgede, med ironisk tilfældighed, over de ødelæggende bølger, som det næsten rørte — i det øjeblik svævede en rød arm og en hammer, løftet bagud i den åbne luft, midt i bevægelsen med at sømme flaget fastere og endnu fastere til den synkende rundholt. En himmelhøg, der hånligt var fulgt med stormasttoppen nedad fra sit naturlige hjem mellem stjernerne og hakkede i flaget og plagede Tashtego dér, kom nu til at lægge sin brede, flagrende vinge mellem hammeren og træet. I samme øjeblik, da han mærkede dette himmelske gys, holdt den nedsunkne vilde nedenunder i sin dødskamp sin hammer frossen dér. Og så sank himlens fugl med ærkeenglelignende skrig, med det kejserlige næb stukket opad og hele sin fangne skikkelse svøbt i Ahabs flag, ned med sit skib. Det var det skib, der ligesom Satan ikke ville synke til helvede, før det havde slæbt en levende del af himlen med sig og hjelmet sig med den.

Nu fløj små fugle skrigende over svælget, som stadig gabede åbent. En mut hvid brænding slog mod dets stejle sider. Så faldt alt sammen, og havets store ligklæde rullede videre, som det havde rullet for fem tusind år siden.
